subject: Creativity
title: Disruptive Innovation: How Small Beats Big
description: A quick win: understand Disruptive Innovation: How Small Beats Big.

hook.text: Netflix didn't beat Blockbuster by being a better video store.

buildup.text: Clayton Christensen's 'disruptive innovation' theory: newcomers enter at the bottom with inferior products, then.

discovery.text: Disruption works because incumbents rationally ignore the low end — the margins are too small.

twist.text: The iPhone disrupted cameras, maps, music players, and flashlights — none of which were its primary market.

climax.text: Christensen predicted that traditional universities would be disrupted by online learning.

punchline.text: The biggest threats to big companies are small companies that don't look.

quiz.question: Why do incumbent companies typically miss disruptive threats?
options: The low-end newcomers have margins too small to notice

details.summary: Clayton Christensen's disruptive innovation theory explains how smaller companies with inferior products can overthrow established giants. Disruption begins at the low end of a market where incumbents do not compete, then improves until it captures the mainstream market.
details.whyItMatters: Disruptive innovation explains why dominant companies regularly fail to see threats from below. Understanding the pattern helps both incumbents protect themselves and challengers find strategic entry points.
takeaways: Disruption starts with inferior products in ignored market segments
Incumbents rationally ignore early disruptors because margins are low
As the disruptor improves, it captures the mainstream market

faq.question: Is every new technology disruptive?
faq.answer: No. Christensen distinguished sustaining innovations that improve existing products for current customers from disruptive innovations that initially serve new or low-end markets. Only the latter constitute true disruption. The term is widely misused.

faq.question: Can incumbents survive disruption?
faq.answer: Some can, by creating separate units that target the disrupting market with its own business model. The main challenge is organizational: the parent company's culture and incentives resist cannibalizing profitable existing products.
